why: An operation copies a '1' one step to the left, so a 0 can become 1 only if some '1' lies to its right. One operation on the nearest such 0 always adds exactly one '1', so the greedy answer is ones + min(k, number of zeros with a '1' to their right).
hints: What must be true about a '0' for any sequence of operations to turn it into a '1'?
A 0 that has a '1' anywhere to its right can be flipped: fill zeros right-to-left starting just left of a '1', and each operation adds exactly one '1'. Zeros after the last '1' can never change.
Scan from the right, counting ones and the zeros seen after at least one '1'. Return ones + min(k, those zeros). O(n), O(1).
pitfalls: Trailing zeros after the last '1' are lost causes.
An all-zero string stays at 0 whatever k is.
k = 0 just counts the existing ones.
